Agentic RAG vs. RAG: Why Your Retrieval Pipeline Needs to Start Reasoning

AI Agents · Chatbots · LLMs · AI

Agentic RAG Systems

A support agent asks your AI assistant why their invoice changed this month. Your RAG pipeline embeds the question, pulls back a generic help article about how billing works, and confidently tells the customer nothing useful — because the actual answer was sitting in a SQL table it never queried. This is the failure mode that’s quietly pushing every serious RAG system toward something more agentic: retrieval that reasons about what it’s missing instead of retrieving once and hoping.

What is RAG?

2023 RAG, or traditional RAG, is a technique where an AI model retrieves information from a knowledge base and generates its response. The AI queries a knowledge base, retrieves information, and then generates a response.

The pipeline is a straight line, and the diagram above shows exactly how short it is: encode your documents and index them in a vector database — commonly Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, or just pgvector inside an existing Postgres instance — encode the incoming query the same way, run a similarity search to pull back the most similar documents, and hand that retrieved context — plus the original query — to the LLM as a single prompt. Seven steps, one pass, done. There’s no step in that flow where the system stops to ask “was that actually the right context?”

That’s the gap agentic RAG was built to close.

What is agentic RAG?

Modern RAG, or agentic RAG, is more dynamic. The AI agent actively manages how it gets information, integrating RAG into a reasoning loop. It’s no longer just retrieving — it’s constantly refining its queries using reasoning. It’s a more intelligent system now. The system decides whether to retrieve, what to retrieve, how many times to retrieve, and when to stop — the same way a person would re-search Google after skimming the first result and realizing it needs more evidence to answer the question.

You can see that reasoning play out in the diagram above. The agent doesn’t just embed and search — it rewrites the initial query, asks itself “do I need more details?”, decides which source will actually help (vector database, tools/API, or the open internet), retrieves, and then — critically — asks a second question before it ever shows the user anything: “is the answer relevant?” If the answer is no, it loops back and tries again rather than shipping a weak response. That evaluate-and-retry cycle, steps 9 through 12 in the diagram, is the piece traditional RAG simply doesn’t have.

The practical trigger for going agentic is query complexity. If your queries are single-hop and unambiguous, a straight traditional retrieval pipeline is cheaper and just as accurate — agentic loops add latency and orchestration cost without a quality payoff. Agentic RAG is at its best when you have multi-hop questions, ambiguous intent, tasks that span multiple data sources, or workflows where the agent must also act.

Why do AI agents need access to dynamic knowledge?

To see why that loop matters, it helps to zoom out from RAG specifically and look at what AI agents are built to do in the first place — and why a fixed snapshot of information was never going to be enough for them.

AI agents are sophisticated AI systems designed to operate on their own. They’re “information robots” that “perceive, reason, plan, and act,” as NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has described them. These agents understand problems, make plans, use different tools, and understand different types of information — text, images, structured data.

An AI agent’s core capabilities break down into four pieces:

  • Perceiving / Query understanding — understanding their surroundings and the context of a situation.
  • Reasoning — breaking down complex problems and strategizing solutions.
  • Planning — creating a step-by-step path to a goal.
  • Acting — executing tasks by using different tools.

Every one of those four depends on information that’s actually current. A model’s training data is a snapshot — frozen at a point in time — but the things an agent gets asked about keep moving: prices change, tickets get resolved, policies get updated, inventory shifts by the hour. An agent that can only pull from a fixed, one-time retrieval has no way to perceive the current state of anything — it’s reasoning over a photograph while the world it’s describing has already moved on. That’s what “dynamic” knowledge means here: not just more data, but data the agent can go re-check at the moment it’s actually needed.

An agent that can only retrieve once, from one source, with no way to judge what came back, isn’t really doing any of that reasoning or planning either — it’s just running a lookup. Both problems point in the same direction: retrieval needs to be something the agent actively controls, not a single step it passes through once.

Why was agentic RAG needed?

Zoom back into retrieval specifically, and the traditional pipeline starts showing cracks against those expectations. There were several recurring issues with the traditional RAG system:

  • No query decomposition: Complex, multi-part questions get embedded as a single vector. The retriever returns a mishmash of loosely related chunks that don’t cleanly address any individual sub-question.
  • No validation: The pipeline can’t evaluate whether retrieved chunks are actually relevant. Irrelevant context gets passed directly to the LLM, which generates plausible but unsupported answers — contributing to hallucinations on anything multi-hop.
  • Single-source constraint: Standard pipelines connect to one knowledge base. If your answer requires data from a vector store, a SQL database, and a live API, you have to build that orchestration yourself.
  • No retry logic: If the first retrieval attempt misses, there’s no mechanism to reformulate and try again. You get one shot.

These are structural limitations, not edge cases — and they’re exactly why agentic RAG has caught on so fast.

How agentic RAG addresses those limitations

Agentic RAG systems replace that fixed pipeline with an agent-controlled loop. It cycles through planning, retrieval, evaluation, and refinement until it has enough evidence to generate an answer. Each of the four limitations above maps to a specific piece of that loop.

Query decomposition and source routing

Query decomposition replaces single-vector embedding. Instead of collapsing a multi-part question into one embedding and hoping the nearest neighbors happen to cover every part of it, the agent first reasons about the question’s structure. Each sub-query gets routed to the most appropriate source. Rather than being wired to one vector store, the agent treats retrieval itself as a decision: which source is likely to have this answer? Factual lookups go to structured databases. Semantic queries go to vector stores. Time-sensitive questions go to web search or live APIs.

This routing decision is itself an LLM call. The agent acts as a classifier, examining each sub-question and selecting from its available tools. In practice, you define these tools explicitly, and the agent’s instructions tell it when to use each one — this is exactly the pattern frameworks like LangGraph and LlamaIndex are built to orchestrate: LlamaIndex typically owns the retrieval side (indexing, chunking, source connectors), while LangGraph handles the routing and state management around it.

Multi-hop retrieval

Some questions require chaining multiple retrieval steps, where the output of one informs the input to the next. RAG agents handle this by maintaining a scratchpad of intermediate results. After each retrieval, the agent decides whether it has enough context or needs to retrieve more. Systems like RQ-RAG formalize this by decomposing multi-hop queries into ordered sub-questions. RAG-Fusion takes a parallel approach instead, generating multiple reformulations of the same query and merging results using reciprocal rank fusion to improve recall.

Self-correction and retrieval validation

In a traditional pipeline, whatever the retriever returns goes straight to the LLM. The model can’t tell good context from bad. Agentic RAG adds a validation step: the agent scores each retrieved chunk for relevance before deciding whether to include it, discard it, or re-query.

This self-correction is what really distinguishes agentic retrieval from the traditional pipeline. The agent treats retrieved data as evidence to evaluate, not ground truth. When chunks conflict, the agent can retrieve additional context to resolve the contradiction rather than passing the conflict straight to the LLM and hoping for the best.

Reflection and memory

Advanced agentic RAG systems add two mechanisms on top of the retrieval loop. Reflection lets the agent review its draft answer, identify gaps or weak support, and trigger additional retrieval if needed. Memory operates at two levels: short-term memory tracks what’s already been retrieved in the current session (avoiding redundant calls), while long-term memory stores patterns from past queries to improve future routing and decomposition.

Putting it together: a concrete example

Say a customer support agent gets asked: “Why did my invoice change this month, and is this a known billing bug?”

A traditional RAG pipeline embeds that whole sentence as one vector, searches a single knowledge base (probably a help-docs vector store), and generates an answer from whatever comes back — usually a generic article about how invoicing works, with no actual answer about this customer’s this invoice.

An agentic system handles it differently, step by step:

  1. Decomposition — the agent splits the question into two sub-queries: “what changed on this customer’s invoice this month?” and “is there a known billing bug matching this change?”
  2. Routing — the first sub-query goes to the billing SQL database (structured, factual). The second goes to the vector store holding engineering/support docs (semantic).
  3. Multi-hop chaining — the SQL result comes back showing a line-item price increase. That detail becomes part of the input to the second retrieval, so the doc search is now specifically about that line item, not billing in general.
  4. Validation — the agent checks the retrieved doc against the SQL result. If the doc says the bug was already patched two weeks ago, but the SQL data shows the change happened yesterday, the agent flags the contradiction and re-queries — checking the support ticket system for a possible recurrence — instead of confidently telling the customer it’s a known, already-fixed bug.

That’s the whole loop from the diagrams above, applied to one real question: decompose, route, chain, validate, and only then answer. A traditional pipeline can’t do any of steps 2 through 4 — it has one vector store and one shot.

Designing an agentic RAG system with reasoning

Once you’ve decided you need that loop, there are still several architectural choices to make. The right one depends on query complexity, data structure, and your latency budget.

Query planning and decomposition strategies

The simplest approach is prompt-based decomposition: the agent is instructed to break a complex query into sub-queries before retrieving. More sophisticated systems use a dedicated planning step, where the agent generates a full retrieval plan up front.

Plan-and-execute architectures separate the planner from the executor. The planner reasons through the full task and produces a step-by-step plan. The executor runs each step and returns results to the planner for evaluation. This separation cuts costs, because the executor can run on a smaller, faster model while the planner handles the heavier reasoning.

Graph RAG and structured knowledge sources

Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph from your documents and retrieves via graph traversal instead of similarity search. For domains where information is inherently relational, graph-based agentic retrieval consistently outperforms flat vector retrieval on complex reasoning tasks.

The tradeoff is that knowledge graphs are expensive to build and maintain. They work best for stable, high-value datasets, where the upfront investment in graph construction pays off over many queries.

Routing agents, ReAct agents, and plan-and-execute agents

Three agent patterns show up most often in agentic RAG systems:

  • Routing agents — a routing agent examines the query and selects the most appropriate retrieval tool or data source. It doesn’t plan multi-step workflows, it just picks a lane.
  • ReAct agents — ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) agents interleave thinking and tool use. The agent reasons about what to do, takes an action, evaluates the result, and reasons about the next step. This pattern handles open-ended queries well but can get expensive, since it makes multiple LLM calls per iteration.
  • Plan-and-execute agents — these separate planning from execution entirely. The planning agent produces a full workflow up front. The execution agent runs each step without calling back to the planner until it finishes or hits an error. Completion rates tend to be higher and costs lower, because the executor isn’t re-planning at every step.

You rarely build these primitives from scratch. LangGraph is the common choice when you need durable, stateful orchestration with checkpointing across long-running loops. CrewAI has the lowest barrier to entry for role-based, multi-agent setups if you’re prototyping a routing or plan-and-execute pattern quickly. AutoGen leans toward multi-agent conversational patterns, where a supervisor agent delegates to specialist agents and synthesizes their results. For graph-based retrieval specifically, Microsoft’s open-source GraphRAG is the reference implementation most teams start from.

Monitor, evaluate, and debug agentic RAG pipelines

All of that extra reasoning comes with an extra burden: agentic RAG systems introduce multiple points of failure that single-pass RAG simply doesn’t have. Retrieval accuracy alone accounts for roughly 60% of RAG quality variance — the rest comes down to how well the generator processes and uses the context it’s given. Evaluating only the retrieval step leaves major blind spots in system performance. A system can retrieve perfect context and still produce a wrong or fabricated answer — this is called the “accuracy fallacy,” where a pipeline looks healthy end-to-end while quietly hallucinating.

Every agent run involves multiple LLM calls, tool invocations, and retrieval steps. You need traces that capture the full chain: what query the agent decomposed, which tools it called, what each tool returned, how the agent evaluated relevance, and what it decided to do next. Without end-to-end traces, debugging a bad answer means guessing which step went wrong.

That means tracking metrics at every layer, not just the final output. Tools like Ragas, DeepEval, and TruLens ship prebuilt scorers for most of these out of the box, and platforms like LangSmith or Arize Phoenix handle the end-to-end tracing across LLM calls and tool invocations:

  • Context precision — are the retrieved chunks actually relevant to the query?
  • Context recall — were all the chunks needed for a complete answer retrieved? (This is where multi-hop questions quietly fail — the generator answers fluently from partial context while precision-only dashboards stay green.)
  • Faithfulness — is the generated answer supported by the retrieved context, with no fabricated claims?
  • Answer relevance — does the answer actually address what the user asked?
  • Hallucination — a reference-free safety net scored on the final output alone.

Guardrails for prompt injection and output validation are just as important. Agentic RAG systems are vulnerable to prompt injection because the agent incorporates retrieved text directly into its reasoning context — a malicious document sitting in your knowledge base could hijack the agent’s behavior. Output guardrails validate that generated answers stay within expected bounds: no leaked system prompts, no fabricated citations, no off-topic responses.

The other layer worth implementing is hybrid search validation — confirming that semantic search results and keyword-based retrieval return consistent, non-contradictory context before synthesis. When the two diverge significantly, that’s usually a signal to re-query rather than merge conflicting evidence.

Production tradeoffs and when not to use agentic RAG

None of this makes agentic RAG a strict upgrade over traditional RAG. The benefits and the engineering cost need to be weighed against each other.

Latency and cost overhead of iterative retrieval

Every iteration in the agent’s loop involves at least one LLM call and one retrieval call. A multi-hop query that requires three retrieval cycles costs roughly three times as much as single-pass retrieval, and takes proportionally longer.

Complexity of agent orchestration at scale

More agents mean more failure modes. RAG agents can select the wrong tool, enter infinite retry loops, or produce inconsistent results across runs. Multi-agent systems introduce coordination overhead on top of that: agents can compete for resources, deadlock on shared state, or produce conflicting intermediate results.

Feedback loops that surface retrieval failures back to the planner are essential here. Without them, a subtle ingestion error or a stale index goes undetected until a user surfaces a bad answer.

Choosing between simple RAG and agentic RAG

Put together, that’s a practical decision framework:

Traditional RAG isn’t a lesser version of agentic RAG — it’s the right tool when your questions are simple and your data lives in one place, and no amount of looping fixes a problem you don’t actually have. Agentic RAG earns its cost when the question itself demands it: multiple sources, multiple hops, or an answer that needs to be checked before it’s trusted. The real skill isn’t picking a side — it’s building the simple pipeline first, watching where it actually breaks on real user queries, and adding just enough of the loop to fix that specific gap. That’s a more durable approach than architecting for complexity you’re guessing you’ll need.
